title: Reverse-Item Disaster
summary: A six-item fictional scale with two reverse-keyed items, scored four ways: correctly, with no recoding, with the wording reversed mentally but not in the data, and with the wrong scale maximum. Totals, item-total correlations, alpha and the respondent ranking all update, and a step-by-step repair mode has students do the arithmetic themselves.
learningObjectives: Recode a reverse-keyed item correctly for a given scale range.
Recognise a negative corrected item-total correlation as the signature of a scoring failure.
Explain why the wrong-maximum error is harder to detect than forgetting to recode entirely.
Distinguish understanding an item as reversed from recoding its numeric response.
State the costs of reverse wording as well as its benefits.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native select, radios, number input and buttons throughout. Every item states its keying in words ('Reverse-keyed') rather than by tint alone, and every recoded answer cell prints the transformation as text ('5 to 1'). The profile chart is hidden from assistive technology and each bar is labelled in text with whether it is the correct or the currently scored total. The repair input accepts Enter as well as the button, and distinguishes the wrong-maximum error and the untouched-number error with specific feedback rather than a generic wrong. Item-total correlations are given a written reading ('negative — flags a problem'). Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Reverse-keyed items: correct recoding, the errors that leave no trace, and why reverse wording is a trade rather than a free fix
simulationNotes: Six original items about persistence written for this tool, answered 1-5 by six fictional respondents whose answers were chosen so the true ordering is unambiguous under correct scoring. No published scale, item or dataset is reproduced. Cronbach's alpha and corrected item-total correlations are computed from the six cases and are illustrative only: statistics from six respondents are wildly unstable and the figures show a direction rather than a magnitude. Four scoring methods are implemented, including two that are arithmetically identical but represent different mistakes.
